references.label: RCUK 2025 ALS cardioversion
references.citation: Resuscitation Council UK. Adult advanced life support guidelines 2025. Tachyarrhythmias: synchronised cardioversion.
references.excerpt: For atrial fibrillation: An initial synchronised shock at maximum defibrillator output, rather than an escalating approach, is a reasonable strategy based on current data. For atrial flutter and paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia: Give an initial shock of 70-120 J. For ventricular tachycardia with a pulse: Use energy levels of 120-150 J for the initial shock.

references.label: CCM 2000 Proarrhythmia
references.citation: Kowey PR, Marinchak RA, Rials SJ, Filart RA. Classification and pharmacology of antiarrhythmic drugs. Antiarrhythmic agents and proarrhythmia. Crit Care Med. 2000;28(10 Suppl):N129-N135.
references.excerpt: The Vaughn Williams classification divides antiarrhythmic agents into four groups according to their effects on various ion channels. Class I agents block sodium channels and are subdivided into three groups. Class Ib agents include lidocaine, which is extensively used for the acute treatment of ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Class Ic drugs are not advisable for patients with structural cardiac abnormalities.

references.label: JACC 2023 Electrical Storm
references.citation: Elsokkari I, Sapp JL, et al. Multidisciplinary critical care management of electrical storm: JACC state-of-the-art review. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2023;81(22):2189-2206.
references.excerpt: Electrical storm (ES) reflects life-threatening cardiac electrical instability with 3 or more ventricular arrhythmia episodes within 24 hours. Identification of underlying arrhythmogenic cardiac substrate and reversible triggers is essential. Medical management includes antiarrhythmic drugs, beta-adrenergic blockade, sedation, and hemodynamic support.

cards.question: Outline the Vaughan-Williams classification with examples.
cards.answer: Class I — Na⁺ channel blockers: Ia (procainamide, quinidine — moderate block, prolong AP), Ib (lidocaine — fast block, shortens AP, ventricular only), Ic (flecainide — strong block, no AP change). Class II — β-blockers (atenolol, esmolol). Class III — K⁺ channel blockers prolonging AP (amiodarone, sotalol). Class IV — Ca²⁺ channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem). Adenosine and digoxin sit outside this classification.

cards.question: What is the management of unstable AF in theatre?
cards.answer: Unstable (chest pain, hypotension, heart failure, syncope): synchronised DC cardioversion — for AF an initial shock at maximum defibrillator output rather than an escalating approach, for atrial flutter/SVT 70–120 J, and for VT with a pulse 120–150 J (RCUK 2025). Stable: rate control with β-blocker (esmolol, metoprolol) or calcium-channel blocker (avoid in heart failure); amiodarone 300 mg IV over 30 min if needs rhythm control or rate control fails. Anticoagulation considered if AF >48 h or known chronic. Look for and treat precipitants — hypoxia, electrolytes, sepsis, ischaemia, fluid overload.

cards.question: Why is amiodarone used despite its toxicity profile?
cards.answer: Highly effective for both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias; minimal negative inotropy; safe in heart failure. Toxicity (often dose-/duration-related): pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, thyroid dysfunction (contains iodine — both hyper- and hypo-), corneal microdeposits, photosensitivity, peripheral neuropathy. Long half-life ~50 days (huge Vd ~70 L/kg). IV: 5 mg/kg over 30 min via central line (peripheral causes thrombophlebitis); 300 mg push in cardiac arrest after 3rd shock.
